text: This is a coupled routing decision. Collecting on either side allows the chassis to translate across a fuel pile while its fixed shooter points toward the destination. That can recover some of the directional independence normally purchased with a turret. A four-bar can also move backward under a frontal impact, but only if the linkage, motor controller, chain and hard stops permit that motion. More joints create more wear locations, and both collectors consume the space that another architecture could use for a hopper. The second intake should therefore be evaluated by additional useful fuel delivered, rather than the visual symmetry of the mechanism.

text: Adding a fourth release lane helps only if four lanes remain supplied. A floor feeding a narrow or irregular throat produces alternating bursts and starvation even when the drum has ample power. Low-friction backing reduces the energy lost to sliding while powered rollers maintain forward contact. An open path also needs a controlled final approach: a ball entering the launch contact at a variable velocity or height changes compression and the exit state. Diagnose the last few balls separately from the first dense volley.

text: A drum’s useful contact surface is a distributed launch interface. If fuel encounters different compression along its width, the nominally identical lanes can launch at different speeds. Flywheel energy can cover short impulses while the motors replace average energy, but a dense volley still requires sufficient sustained electrical power. Surface condition, ball wear and hood contact determine how much of the wheel’s speed becomes translation versus spin. The reported rate is valuable as a team result; it does not establish accuracy, defended performance, battery condition or an all-match average. Copy the geometry only with a plan to characterize those conditions.

text: The expanding walls and intake form one mechanism state machine. A wall that expands independently without managing its overlap can create a ledge, trap fuel, or fight the intake during retraction. Smooth fasteners reduce snagging, while the deployed catches react loads that should not be carried continuously by the intake motor. A large hopper helps separate acquisition from discharge, giving the driver freedom to reposition. That freedom disappears if the final fuel cannot leave without a specific intake movement. The recommendation should therefore specify both the retained capacity and the emptying sequence.

A mechanism database needs this control contract because an intake, indexer and drum borrowed from different robots may otherwise disagree about who owns the next ball.

text: These capacity figures describe different operating envelopes, not one universally available volume. Coupling deployment to the collector saves an actuator and synchronizes the opening, but also couples hopper faults to pickup. A good borrowed implementation preserves service access and allows the robot to recover when only one side deploys correctly.

text: A belt bed pulls continuously on its support shafts; the tension required to transmit power can bend those shafts even before fuel loading is considered. A roller floor moves that challenge into shaft spacing, surface grip and transmission design. Agitation is not automatically helpful: repeated upward kicks can keep a ball from settling into the receiving contact. This is why a rate test must observe the inlet to the superstructure, not only the speed of the floor.

text: This is direct team evidence for treating climb as a low-priority 2026 architecture choice. Its cost is larger than its actuator and hook: it can remove storage, require alignment practice, complicate wiring and consume testing that could improve fuel flow. The agent should begin with the observed fuel-dominant game, then require a specific positive marginal case before adding climb. It should not recommend one merely because the manual awards points for it.

A compact throat earns hopper space only if it remains serviceable and can clear a hard jam.

The controller needs the correct state at release, not merely a final position, because angle and velocity together determine the shot. This is a specific tested alternative, not a claim that catapults universally beat flywheels.

A tube can press a belt into a support, climb at one end while the other end remains constrained, or stop a roller whose structure is bent. Each mode requires a different change. A useful agent should first ask which contacts stop moving and where the tube becomes over-constrained; recommending more torque without this observation can destroy the part that reveals the fault.

text: A bulk pile can load the singulator even when the exit path is clear. Agitating the pile and supplying the launch stream are different motions, so separating drives gives useful tuning freedom. A shaped fin can alter where that pile pressure is released; passive rollers reduce sliding resistance where balls push against each other. These details explain why a DYE-inspired design cannot be generalized as a generic circular indexer. The critical behavior is the changing network of contacts at full, partial and nearly empty loads, including a controlled reverse to clear a bridge.

text: A compact turret can improve the whole robot by leaving more feed and storage volume around its swept envelope.
